claims.text: The untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy is single-phase BCC.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C.
Untreated NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
Irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has previously been predicted by first-principles calculations.
Introducing approximately 5 at% V into NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility.
Approximately 5 at% V lowers the Peierls barrier to dislocation motion at room temperature.
V incorporation promotes additional active slip systems.
Vanadium is a more ductile refractory element whose behavior can be transferred to NbMoTaW.
V atoms introduce minor lattice distortions into the BCC lattice.
The V-induced lattice distortions facilitate low-temperature dislocation motion.
An approximately 5 at% V addition can retain a single-phase BCC microstructure.
The controlled small V addition will not trigger secondary-phase formation.
The V-modified alloy will have a higher room-temperature strain-to-failure than untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will retain mechanical performance similar to untreated NbMoTaW at 1600 °C.
The V-modified alloy will show no deleterious change in irradiation resistance relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Preserving a single-phase BCC structure will maintain high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
V additions exceeding approximately 5 at% may cause secondary-phase formation.
Secondary-phase formation caused by excess V could adversely affect room-temperature, high-temperature, and irradiation properties.
The magnitude of any ductility improvement is not known without experimental calibration.
The preservation of high-temperature and irradiation performance is an assumption requiring experimental validation.

contradictions.description: The composition route is inconsistent or underdetermined: some statements specify substitution of one constituent, while the intervention also permits simply adding V. These routes produce different Nb/Mo/Ta/W concentrations, and the constituent to be replaced is never identified.
